storyTitle: Favorite Problems: A Practical Framework for Discovering Your Purpose
text:
Evolution would have that be your purpose, or at least Co-operative evolution  [0] would.
At this point, humanity has partially conquered evolution. You can choose a different purpose than reproduction or fitness of the human species (helping others, as you put it).
There are people who see helping animals and nature as more important than helping other humans.
There are yet more who strive primarily for their own personal wealth/power, to the detriment of mankind and only sometimes with their own progeny in mind.
With that in mind, I think you may wish to also be more specific in your stated purpose. "Help others do their thing" is vague and imprecise. It would allow you equally to use your time and money to support others who's goals are merely to get rich (say, to be an angel investor), and to help others who's goal is likewise to help others (help others improve their lives and better themselves, such as through working at / giving to foodbanks, helping those doing positive work for humanity, etc).
I charitably will read your meaning not to be "help others to do their thing", but rather to "try to have as positive as possible an impact overall, including through helping others". If helping others is done with the intent of having a positive impact, it looks much different. You don't become a VC (the 3rd most evil profession) that optimizes for maximum returns, but instead help fund interests that you genuinely believe will end up being overall positive. You don't help others do their thing unless, as best you can tell, their thing will also have a positive impact on others.
Did you mean something to that effect, or do you see your purpose truly as an amoral helper who wishes to help others but neither impact good yourself (directly nor indirectly), nor discriminate in what "others" and "things" to help?

author: carapace
storyTitle: The New History of the Milky Way
text:
Like most technology, artificial light is a blessing and a curse.
On the one hand you have things like aid programs to give poor folks LED lights so they can read at night (for e.g. kids' education) without burning fuel (typically wood or dung, leading to health problems and ecological degradation), creating "virtuous cycles".  So that's good.
On the other hand, light pollution is so bad that kids grow up never seeing the night sky, effectively they are inside a virtual world.  Shall we become Krikkiters?
( https://sites.google.com/site/h2g2theguide/Index/k/krikkit )
When you look at a picture of the Earth at night from orbit and see the synthetic human mycelium of light spread over the land, it's kind of beautiful, but at the same time all those photons are waste, pollution.  In infrared bands the waste is even more glaring. (That's not a pun, it's literal.)
Also, humans have great night vision.  There's a whole mode where the peripheral vision takes over from the foveal vision and you can see just fine.  It's quite literally like "nightvision" in D&D: you can't see in the actual absence of light, but you can see in starlight.  Also, in this mode you can see luminescent fungi and bugs and such clearly.  There was an article in the old "Whole Earth Quarterly" (which I think is now online and maybe searchable somewhere, so maybe I can dig it up...) about folks experimenting with this.  They made hats with a bit of clothes-hanger-wire attached and a dot of glow-in-the-dark paint, such that the dot of luminescence was in the air in front of their eyes and, um, several inches (?) away.  The method was to go into a natural (dark but not deep-forest-pitch-black) area, put on the hat, let the eyes fixate on the dot (to prevent you trying to look around with your foveal cells) and then direct your attention to your peripheral field of view (basically everything from the foveal "sweet spot", which is actually quite small,  IIRC the size of your fist on your outstretched arm, to the sides of your head.  Humans can see nearly 180°.  You can test this yourself.  Put up your arm and do a thumbs' up gesture.  Wiggle your thumb as you move your arm to the side while looking straight ahead (don't move your eyes or head.)  You should be able to see the motion to nearly 90°.)  Anyhow, the folks in that article were running around in the woods and fields at night with no flashlights.  Literally running.  I'll see if I can dig up the link later today.
(Not to rant, but these new LED street lights and car head lights (and bike lights too) are blinding.  They hurt my eyes!)

Exactly, that's what a "fixed point" is.
Fun fact about fixed points #1: Put a sheet of paper on a desk. Notice the precise area of the desk's surface that it covers. Now ball up the sheet of paper however you wish, without tearing it. Put it down again in such a way that every part of that sheet is somewhere over the original area that the paper occupied. Then there is at least one point on the paper that is precisely above its original location.
Fun fact about fixed points #2: Some functions, even simple ones suitable for a desktop calculator, do not reliably approach a fixed point when applied repeatedly to their own output. You can see this in action at Wikipedia "Cobweb plot" (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobweb_plot) for the function known as the "logistic map", y = rx(1-x). Varying the initial value of x (really, x-subscript-zero) and the parameter r can cause the map to converge to a fixed point, to enter a repeating sequence of any length, or to remain in a finite range without ever repeating. This last behavior is known as "chaos".
